questions.q: In the Deutsch-Jozsa promise problem for f : {0,1}^n -> {0,1}, what two possibilities is f guaranteed to be one of?
options: Periodic or aperiodic
Constant (same output on every input) or balanced (output 0 on exactly half the domain and 1 on the other half)
Linear or quadratic
Invertible or non-invertible
questions.explain: The promise rules out every function that is neither constant nor balanced -- those are the only two cases the algorithm needs to distinguish between.

questions.q: For the n = 1 circuit, what is the exact final state when f is constant-0 (f(0)=0, f(1)=0), and what is P(input qubit measures 0)?
questions.explain: The verified simulation gives this exact state for constant-0, with all amplitude on input-bit-0 terms, so the input qubit measures 0 with certainty.

questions.q: Why does measuring the input qubit as |1> after this circuit certify, with certainty, that f is balanced?
options: Because the ancilla qubit directly encodes the answer, independent of the input qubit
Because for both balanced functions (identity and NOT), the final state has exactly zero amplitude on every term where the input bit is 0, so P(input=1) = 1.0000 exactly
Because the measurement is only probabilistic, giving roughly a 50% chance either way
Because balanced functions are simply more common than constant functions
questions.explain: For balanced-identity and balanced-NOT, the verified final states have zero amplitude on all input=0 terms, making P(input=1) exactly 1.0000, not merely likely.

questions.q: What is the classical worst-case query count needed to decide constant-vs-balanced for a general n-bit promise function, and how does it compare to the quantum query count?
options: Classical worst case needs n queries; quantum needs n/2 queries
Classical worst case needs 2^(n-1) + 1 queries; quantum needs exactly 1 query regardless of n
Classical worst case needs 2 queries; quantum needs 1 query, the same gap for every n
Classical and quantum both need exactly 1 query for any n
questions.explain: Querying up to half the domain can still leave the answer ambiguous; one more than half (2^(n-1)+1) is required classically, while the quantum circuit always needs exactly 1 query no matter how large n is.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe Deutsch-Jozsa's advantage as historically important but practically limited, unlike Grover's or Shor's algorithm?
options: The algorithm has never been verified by simulation, unlike Grover's or Shor's

The constant-vs-balanced promise is an artificial setup built specifically to produce the separation, and doesn't correspond to a function type that arises in a real problem anyone needs solved, unlike unstructured search or integer factoring
Deutsch-Jozsa's speedup is actually larger than Shor's, which makes it less interesting
Deutsch-Jozsa only works on classical computers, not quantum ones
questions.explain: The query-complexity separation is real and provable, but it's demonstrated on a deliberately artificial promise problem rather than a practical computational task, unlike Grover's real search speedup or Shor's real factoring speedup.
